messages.subject: VCP, high densities, snapshot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Distance-samplers,
I have been using VCP counts to assess songbird densities in German
forested areas as described by BIBBY et al. 1992 (two bands, 0-30 m and
30 m - infinity; counting period 6 and 10 min., resp.). The resulting
densities were far to high (factor 3 or so compared to expected densities
from 'normal' territory mapping results in literature), as already
experienced by BIBBY et al. 1985.
BIBBY et al. 2000 and BUCKLAND et al. 2001 address the problem of high
densities and advocate for snapshot techniques and the use of precise
distance measurements for each individual recorded. As I only found
general hints on this topic in both works, I would very much like to know
about quantitative considerations on errors comparing e.g. 10 min. full
count vs. snapshot and two counting bands vs. precise distance. Can
missing snapshots/precise distances be considered a satisfying explanation
for those high densities ?
Any comments or hints on citable references will be highly appreciated.
Greetings,
Wilken

References:

BIBBY, C.J., BURGESS, N.D. & HILL, D.A. 1992. Bird Census Techniques.
Academic Press, London.

BIBBY, C.J., BURGESS, N.D., HILL, D.A., MUSTOE, S.H. 2000. Bird Census
Techniques. 2nd Ed. Academic Press, London.

BIBBY, C.J., PHILLIPS, B.N. & SEDDON, A.J. 1985. Birds of restocked
conifer plantations in Wales. Journal of Applied Ecology 22: 619-633.

BUCKLAND, S.T., ANDERSON, D.R., BURNHAM, K.P., LAAKE, J.L., BORCHERS, D.L.
& THOMAS, L. 2001. Introduction into Distance Sampling. Oxford University
Press, Oxf.

messages.subject: Re: VCP, high densities, snapshot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Wilken and group,

Of general interest perhaps is a newly published paper by T. R. Shankar Raman
comparing bird counting techniques in a (tropical) forest. It's in the January
issue of Ibis (2003) vol. 145: pp. 9-21.

He concluded that 'inflated' density estimates from VCPM were a product of
bird movement during the count period. While such movement should be a
problem, especially in 10 minute counts, I'm not sure the above paper
quantifies the overall effect very accurately - there may even be greater
errors (underestimation) in the territory mapping (which he uses as the
baseline of 'true' density) than there are in the distance sampling methods.

I have seen almost nothing in the literature on the quest for compromise point
count periods that minimise bias due to bird movement, while at the same time
maintaining detection probability over crucial distances. Optimum count
periods should vary between bird groups and between habitats. Maybe someone on
the list knows of work on this?

Dr Stuart J. Marsden
Senior Lecturer in Biogeography and Conservation Biology
Applied Ecology Group
Department of Environmental and Geographical Sciences
Manchester Metropolitan University
Chester Street
Manchester M1 5GD

tel: 0161 247 6215
fax: 0161 247 6318

http://www.egs.mmu.ac.uk/users/mdobson/Marsden/Marsden.html

messages.subject: VCP, high densities, snapshot
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

Yes, I agree with Stuart that optimal counting periods for point-transects
do vary per species.  During a study I was conducting in New Zealand
temperate rain forest, I believed that a five-minute counting period was
overestimating abundances for honeyeaters, and started experimenting with
snapshot counts.  These snapshot counts were executed after a three minute
waiting and observing period - they consistently yielded lower estimates
of density for my faster moving species.

In contrast I found that this snapshot technique was woefully inadequate
for species such as our large endemic wood pigeon - for which even up to a
ten minute period was more suitable due to their frequently silent and
still presence in the canopy.  These pigeons are also generally extremely
noisy when entering, leaving, or moving within the point transect area and
therefore over-estimations of density due to undetected movement during
the long count were not a problem.

I'm currently whipping a paper into shape and hope to submit these results
for publication in the near future.

In fact the importance of taking the time to determine how best to apply
distance techniques on a species specific basis can not be overemphasized:
 Another paper (on which I was just a co-author) that has ben submitted to
Ibis, showed line-transects to perform extremely well on a NZ passerine
of known population size.  Whereas, both one-minute and five-minute
point-transects vastly overestimated population estimates. -- However,
these point-transect counts were conducted after a five-minute standing,
waiting, period and I believe that this slightly curious species may have
been inclined to move towards a standing observer - and subsequently,
that these over inflated point-transect results may be an example of the
dramatic effect that movement towards the observer can have on estimates
of density.  I am following up on this and will be trying to establish
whether or not these birds do indeed react in this way to a standing
observer.

Cheers, Rosemary

messages.subject: Announce: Distance 4 Release 2
messages.body_plain:
Distance samplers,

An updated release of Distance 4.0 is now available for download from the
Distance web site

              http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

The new release (Release 2) fixes several problems that the developers and
users identified in Release 1, and includes a few minor new features (see
below for details).  Thanks to everyone who reported a problem or suggested a
feature.

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland

New Features

Analysis: In Model Definition | Detection Function | Diagnostics when
specifying manual selection of intervals can now specify automatic equal
cutpoints between left and right truncation distances by leaving the values
in cutpoints table as 0 (see manual).

Analysis: Cluster size is now a decimal field in the Project Setup Wizard,
and non-integer cluster sizes can be analyzed in the CDS and MCDS analysis
engines.  (This was actually introduced in Release 1, but was not
documented.)

Analysis: Sample size for estimating the detection function is reported as
non-integer when smearing is used.  Also, observed sample sizes in GOF tables
are non-integer when there is smearing.  Note that sample size for cluster
size regression is still integer, as the observed distances are used in this
regression   this means that the number of observations for cluster size
regression can be different from the number of observations for the detection
function fitting.  One issue still to resolve here is whether smearing works
with the MCDS engine (problem 217).

Analysis: For objects in clusters, you can now include objects where cluster
size is not known in the analysis.  To avoid bias, the average probability of
detection for objects with missing cluster size must be the same as for
objects with known cluster size.  To include these objects, code them as
cluster size 0.  When you run the analysis, a warning will be issued, and
objects will cluster size 0 will be used in estimating the detection function
and in encounter rate calculations, but not in cluster size estimation.  This
feature is not documented in the manual as it is preliminary, and may be
withdrawn in a future build.  Please let us know if you encounter any
problems using it.

Project Setup: When setting up a project for analysis, a default data filter,
model definition and analysis are created as part of setting up the project
when you click  Finish .  Any multiplier fields defined in the Setup Project
Wizard are now included in the default model definition, including cue count
multipliers.  The default analysis is a CDS analysis   if you change to MCDS
then you ll have to re-define the multipliers yourself.

Resolved Problems

Interface

{35} Data Filter Properties, Data Selection tab. Allows you to specify the
same layer type more than once.
{109} Data Filter Properties, Data Selection tab. Selection criteria column
stays grey when you re-open the properties   should be white for rows
containing criteria.  [LJT; 29 March 01; Fixed LJT 4 Feb 2003]
{43} Details Windows: When you click on the x box having edited a text box
(e.g., Name) the contents are not saved (loose focus event not fired). [7 Dec
00; fixed 23 Oct 02, LJT]
{206} Details input windows: could crash Distance by renaming an analysis or
design to the same name as a current one in that set [23 Oct 02, LJT, fixed
23 Oct 02, LJT]
{221} Manual: In distance.pdf, chapter 5 is missing [Ian Westbrooke 26 Feb
03; Fixed LJT 26 Feb 03]
{219} Model Definition Properties: MCDS.  When you specify density by stratum
and detection global, next time you open up the properties it has detection
by stratum ticked as well.  [Dan Pike 3 Feb 2003; Fixed LJT 3 Feb 2003]
{207} Survey details: Changing the name under  Name  had no effect. [23 Oct
02 LJT; Fixed 23 Oct 02, LJT]

Analysis Engines

{200} When using the Data Filter | Units tab to convert between units, get an
un-necessary warning message in the results log:  ** Warning: User is
overriding a conversion factor available in the program. **   [LJT 18 Oct 02;
Fixed LJT 18 Oct 02]
{201} Internal errors 50, 51, 53 or 54 can be generated when selecting among
multiple key functions [LJT 18 Oct 02; Fixed LJT 18 Oct 02]
{202} When Internal errors 50-54 were generated, they do not cause the
analysis to return error status and they are not highlighted in the lower
pane of the Log window [LJT 18Oct 02; Fixed LJT 18 Oct 02]
{205} When number of observations in a stratum/sample is 0, can get a crash:
 forrtl: error (73): floating divide by zero , in Routine ESTOUT. [LJT 21 Oct
02; Fixed LJT 21 Oct 02. Crash occurred when trying to calculate percentage
components of variation.]
{208} When you rename a multiplier or multiplier SE field, and then re-run an
analysis without changing the model definition, you get the error message  **
Error: Unexpected error ** Error Source: InputFileMaker.AppendAnalysisString,
Internal Error number: -2147211505., Internal Error description: "Unexpected
error in Distance Database ,Engine.,Source:
D4DbEng.DataLayer.RecordList,Internal Error number: 3061.,Internal Error
description: "Too few parameters. Expected 2.".   This error could be
clearer! [Alexis Cahill + LJT 5 Nov 2002; Fixed LJT 5 Nov 2002   error
message is now of the form  Error: Multiplier field '[field name]' was not
found in the data layer '[layer name]'.]
{209} Can get  Internal Error 53: Mismatched modules.   or  Internal Error
54: Mismatched stats.   [Martin Raphael 21 Oct 02. Fixed LJT 11 Nov 02]
{210} Analyses don t complete when using smearing.  Just lock up and become
unresponsive.  [Dan Pike and LJT 14/11/02; Fixed LJT 25 Nov 02   problem was
with the WriteValues method in D4Util, but also wrote a workaround in D4.exe]
{212} When no monotonicity constraints were set, could still get the warning
message that Monotonicity constraints were being enforced.  The estimates are
correct   just the output is wrong (i.e., monotonicity constraints were not
being used).  [John Davison 15 Jan 03; Fixed LJT 16 Jan 03]
{214} If under Model Definition, Detection function, Diagnostics you choose
manual selection of intervals, but then don t specify the cutpoints, you can
get errors   ** Error: Interval values for distances are out of order. **
and  ** Error: Due to errors, this GOF command will be ignored. ** , with the
previous command being something like  GOF /Intervals=0,0,0 .  Workaround:
specify cutpoints.  [Rick Camp and Luanne Johnson, Jan 2003; Fixed LJT 23 Jan
2003   interface now interprets all 0 cutpoints as being specification of
number of intervals only and not cutpoint values]
{215} When using smearing, histogram bars did not match the level of the
plotted function [Dan Pike, 27/11/02; Fixed LJT 3 Feb 03]
{216} Smearing could result in sample size for fitting the detection function
(which is now non-integer) being different from sample size used for
calculating degrees of freedom of f(0).  Would only be a problem with large
smearing angle or distance.  [Dan Pike 27/11/02; Fixed LJT 3 Feb 03; I
suspect this problem has been in Distance since smearing was first
introducted to the program, as it was quite an esoteric bug.]
{218} Bootstrap analysis can occasionally hang, causing the analysis to run
forever but using no CPU time.  [Dan Pike 27/11/02; fixed LJT 4 Feb 03; would
happen only when an analysis within the bootstrap returned an error   e.g.,
when there were no observations in a bootstrap resample]
{220} More than 32,767 samples (transects) results in an integer overflow or
array bounds error [Stuart Newson 14/02/03; fixed LJT 14/02/03]
CDS Analysis Engine
{213} One or two too many iterations are being reported, when the Misc option
 Report results for each iteration  is selected.  Doesn t affect the
estimates as these last few iterations have the same parameter estimates [LJT
16 Jan 03; Fixed LJT 16 Jan 03]

MCDS Analysis Engine

{199} ESW and multipler units not output on Density Estimates summary pages
when cluster size is a covariate. [17 Oct 02, LJT; fixed 17 Oct 02 LJT]
{203} When cluster size is a covariate, density estimates don t correctly
take into accound differences between distance, effort and area measurement
units [18 Oct 02, LJT; fixed 18 Oct 02 LJT]
{204} Crashes in function UNIQUE when trying to find the number of unique
entries in a list of size 0. [18 Oct 02, LJT; fixed 18 Oct 02 LJT]

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have to design a monitoring project of a rather elusive bird species,=20
which nests in the pebbly shores of a small Italian river (about 0.6 km=20
large). I think that point counts are recommendable, since these birds are=
=20
very shy and can be detected only using scopes. I would like to avoid any=20
possible disturbance to the nesting birds, thus I think that sampling=20
points should be (systematically) distributed along the river banks. By=20
using this design, however, I have to limit the sampling area in each point=
=20
only to the half-circle toward the river, since this birds do not nest=20
outside the river itself.
I wonder if this design is correct and if it is possible to use Distance to=
=20
plan this survey and calculate coverage probability. Is it possible to=20
force the choice of sampling points only to the boundary of the survey area?

messages.subject: Re: sampling design
messages.body_plain:
> > I have to design a monitoring project of a rather elusive bird species,

> > which nests in the pebbly shores of a small Italian river (about 0.6 km

> > large). I think that point counts are recommendable, since these birds are

> > very shy and can be detected only using scopes. I would like to avoid any

> > possible disturbance to the nesting birds, thus I think that sampling

> > points should be (systematically) distributed along the river banks. By

> > using this design, however, I have to limit the sampling area in each point

> > only to the half-circle toward the river, since this birds do not nest

> > outside the river itself.

This is easily accommodated, by setting the effort for each point to one
half per visit, rather than 1 per visit, or by defining a multiplier, set
equal to one half, BUT ...

> > I wonder if this design is correct and if it is possible to use Distance to

> > plan this survey and calculate coverage probability. Is it possible to

> > force the choice of sampling points only to the boundary of the survey area?

this means that you would be estimating density at (or near) the edge of
the survey area, so the method will underestimate abundance.  (The
assumption that points end up at locations with representative densities,
ensured through random or systematic point placement, is violated by this
design.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: D4 MCDS analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I'm cc'ing your message and my reply to the distance-sampling list, as it's
the kind of question I've been asked before.  Others: don't bother reading if
you're not interested in MCDS (i.e., multiple covariates) analyses.

On Fri, 14 Mar 2003 14:29:33 +0100, Daniel Pike wrote:

> >Hi Len

> >I downloaded the new D4 and was running some covariate analyses. I noticed
> >something strange. For most of the covariates, the AIC is exactly the same.
> >For all of them, the estimated esw is exactly the same. I have a feeling
> >something worse than chance must be involved here...

> >I've attached the file, and look in the set called COV. The one at the top
> >is the simple model, the rest are covariate models. Just doesn't seem
> >possible to me, that the covariates would all result in the same AIC and
ESW.

> >Thanks,

> >Daniel.

For other people's benifit: the analyses you sent use the hazard rate key
function with no covariates.  You started with a CDS analysis (ie no
covariates), and that had AIC 1376.68.  Then you tried different covariates:
BSS, CLOUD, SIGHT and GLARE (all non-factor), all of which had AIC to two
decimal places of 1379.51, and OBS (factor, with 3 levels) which had AIC of
1381.51.

When you look at the results of the covariate analyses you can see that the
results are actually slightly different, just at more than two decimal
places.  In each case, the parameter(s) corresponding to the covariate values
are estimated to be almost zero -- in other words the covariate is having
almost no affect on the analysis.  For example, the BSS covariate, from the
Detection Fct/Global/Model Fitting page:

 Model
    Hazard Rate key, k(y) = 1 - Exp(-(y/s)**-A(2))

    s = A(1) * Exp(fcn(A(3)))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                !

    Parameter A(1) is the intercept of the scale parameter s.
    Parameter A(2) is the power parameter.
    Parameter A(3) is the coefficient of covariate BSS.
       A( 1) bounds = ( 14.000     , 0.10000E+07 )
       A( 2) bounds = ( 1.0000     ,  35000.     )

        Iter   LN(likelihood)    Parameter Values
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
          0   -686.753           336.574        3.00000           0.000000
          1   -686.753           336.574        3.00000      -0.859340E-14
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
       Results:
       Convergence was achieved with    2 function evaluations.
       Final Ln(likelihood) value =  -686.75342
       Akaike information criterion =   1379.5068

Parameter A(3) corresponds to the BSS covariate, and its value is estimated
to be -0.85x10-14 -- pretty small!  On the next page of results, you get a
standard error for this parameter:  0.1204.

Same for all the other covariates, which is explains why ESW, etc for all the
covariate analyses are almost exactly the same.

One thing I did notice, however, is that the maximum likelihood found by the
MCDS analysis is "wrong".  Remember that AIC is -2*Lnl + 2*k where k is the
number of parameters.  In the CDS analysis, k is 2 (2 hazard rate
parameters), and in the non-factor MCDS analyses, k is 3 (2 hazard rate
parameters + the covaraite.  When the covariate is having almost no effect,
we expect the log likelihood for both CDS and MCDS analyses to be almost
exactly the same -- so the AIC for the MCDS analysis should be almost exactly
2 higher than the CDS analysis.  But in this case it wasn't: 1376.68 for CDS
and 1379.51 for MCDS.  It's more than two higher.

This implies that the MCDS analysis isn't finding the maximum likelihood
solution.  CDS and MCDS analysis engines use different algorithms so it is
possible for this to happen.  If you re-run the CDS analysis with the option
"Model Definition | Misc | Report results for each iteration of the fitting
routine" ticked, you can see that it doesn't head straight for the maximum
likelihood solution but that -Lnl actually gets higher in one iteration.  You
can also see that the final parameter estimates for the two hazard rate
parameters are different from the MCDS analyses (they are 301.528 and 2.66381
in the CDS analysis, which gives -Lnl -686.389 -- lower than the -686.753
found by the MCDS routine with parameters 336.574 and 3.000 and the very
small BSS parameter).

A solution is to start the MCDS routine off with the maximum likelihood
estimates from the CDS analysis, and 0.000 for the 3rd parameter (the
covariate parameter).  You set starting values in Model Definition |
Detection Function | Adjustment terms | Manually set starting values.  The
number of parameters in this case is 3, and I entered the values 301.518,
2.66381, and 0.0.  Now I get

        Iter   LN(likelihood)    Parameter Values
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
          0   -686.389           301.528        2.66381           0.000000
          1   -686.386           301.533        2.69137      -0.843569E-03
          2   -686.386           301.533        2.69137      -0.843569E-03
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
       Results:
       Convergence was achieved with    3 function evaluations.
       Final Ln(likelihood) value =  -686.38578
       Akaike information criterion =   1378.7716

so the difference in AIC is 1.994 -- more reasonable.  As you can see -- the
effect of the covariate is still very small.

Bottom line is that in this dataset the covariates don't seem to affect the
detection function.

The trick of using CDS results as starting values for MCDS analyses is a
generally useful one -- indeed I should think about implementing it as the
default in Distance one of these days (will make computations take longer
though).  The problem of not finding the maximim likelihood solution is worse
for hazard rate keys than half-normal (actually, I haven't seen an example
with half normal yet), and worse when you have several adjustment terms.

Cheers,

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Environmental and Ecological Modelling
The Observatory, University of St Andrews, Scotland KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: Sampling Unit
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about resampling for bootstrapped CIs.

In about a 900 sq-km area we surveyed all reclaimed surface mines (129
patches) for 3 species of sparrows using line transects.  Depending on the
size of the patch, there could be 1-many transects.

Two observers conducted surveys, in which only a single observer surveyed
any one patch.  We found that for 1 of 3 species the detection functions
were modeled better if different among observers.

For species where we detected no difference between observers (in the
detection fct), should we resample patches as well as transects, or is
simply resampling transects appropriate?  My inclination is to resample
patches, as well as transects within a patch to incorporate variability
among patches as well variability among transects within a patch.

Thanks,

Duane

Assistant Unit Leader and
Adjunct Assistant Professor of Wildlife Ecology

messages.subject: Re: Sampling Unit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Duane, list,

Loosly speaking, bootstrapping is supposed to give you a handle on the variability
you would expect if you were able to repeat the survey many times on the same
population.  So, to work out which levels to bootstrap you need to think about
what was randomly assigned in your design.

You sampled all of the mines, not a random sample.  So there's no point in
resampling at that level.  Within each mine, you presumably selected transect
locations with some element of randomness (e.g., systematic with random start
point).  So you need to resample at this level.  This isn't going to work too well
for the mines with very few transects, but that's life.  I'm not sure how much of
a problem that will be overall -- perhaps others have some insight here?

I don't think the level of resampling is affected by whether you found observer
differences in the detection function or not.

I'd be interested to hear if others disagree.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: D4 data import speed
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jared, list,

Yes, I agree data import is too slow.  An hour for 10,000 records would be about
normal.

To be honest, I wasn't thinking of such enormous datasets when I designed Distance
4 -- I didn't realize that some people have such a large amount of data until the
ICODS conference in 2001, and that was after many design decisions had been made.
If you use the MCDS engine, you'll also notice that that doesn't scale well to
large datasets.

The reason data import is much slower in D4 than D3.5 is because the database
engine is much more general -- designed to cope with data from many sources such
as GIS data.  However, there is undoubtedly scope to make it more efficient while
keeping the generality.

Speeding up data import is on my To Do list -- for some reason it wasn't on the
Known Problems list on the web site so I've added it.  However, it isn't high
priority compared with getting new functionality (such as double-observer methods
and spatial modelling) into the software.

Speeding up the MCDS engine will happen as part of programming new analysis
engines in the staistical software R, and linking R to Distance.  This is
something we're working on now.

So, no respite for data import in the short term I'm afraid.

 - Len

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
